displayQuote: All things are subject to interpretation; whichever interpretation prevails at a given time is a function of power and not truth

meta.title: Who really said "All things are subject to interpretation… a function of power and not truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No source exists in this form. Nietzsche wrote a real note on perspectivism — 'there are no facts, only interpretations' — but it never says interpretation is a function of power rather than truth. That clause is a modern addition.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All things are subject to interpretation… a function of power and not truth'?
meta.ogDescription: Unsourced. The real Nietzsche note says 'it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations' — and says nothing about power versus truth.

answer.label: Not sourced to Nietzsche in this form
answer.sourceLine: This sentence appears in no published work of Nietzsche’s and in no notebook. There is a real passage behind it — his famous note on perspectivism — but that note says something narrower and more interesting, and it never claims that interpretations prevail through power rather than truth. That clause is somebody else’s.

source.heading: What Nietzsche actually wrote

docMeta.dd: The Will to Power §481; Kaufmann, The Portable Nietzsche (1954)
No source; first appearance not established

source.excerpt: Gegen den Positivismus, welcher bei den Phänomenen stehn bleibt "es giebt nur Thatsachen", würde ich sagen: nein, gerade Thatsachen giebt es nicht, nur Interpretationen.
trail: The circulating sentence has no citation anywhere. Wikiquote files it under Disputed, noting it is often attributed to Nietzsche — especially on social media — but that no citation is ever given Wikiquote ↗.

The passage behind it is the perspectivism note, KSA 12, 7[60]: ‘Against that positivism which stops before phenomena, saying “there are only facts,” I should say: no, it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations.’ The note goes on about drives and a ‘lust to rule’ — the only thread connecting it to power — but it never states that truth-claims prevail by power rather than truth source-check ↗.

Two dating notes worth keeping straight: the note is from autumn 1885–86, not 1888 as usually claimed (the 1888 date comes from a heading in The Portable Nietzsche). And we could not establish any first-print date for the popular sentence — all traceable circulation is quote-aggregator and social-media, post-2000 disputed list ↗.
source.excerptNote: The real note in Nietzsche’s German. Compare it with the sentence in circulation: the famous half (‘only interpretations’) is his; the half that does the ideological work (‘a function of power and not truth’) is not.
source.rightsNote: Mixed, and easy to get wrong. Nietzsche died in 1900, so the German original is public domain worldwide — you may quote and translate KSA 12, 7[60] freely. The popular English sentence has no identified author at all, so there is nobody to credit and nothing to clear; it should simply not be presented as Nietzsche’s. Note separately that Walter Kaufmann’s 1954 English rendering of the real note is in copyright, so quote that briefly with attribution or translate the German yourself. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) really did argue that there are no bare facts, only interpretations, and really was preoccupied with power as a drive underlying thought. That makes this sentence unusually plausible — it is a fair summary of a position often ascribed to him. But a summary of someone’s philosophy is not a quotation from it, and this one adds a claim about power and truth that his actual note does not make.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a harder case than an outright fake, because half of it is real. A genuine Nietzschean idea has been fused with a claim he did not make, and the join is invisible unless you go back to the note.

items.who: ‘a function of power and not truth’
items.why: The real note argues that facts do not exist independently of interpretation. It does not say that whichever interpretation wins does so through power rather than truth — a much stronger, and much more usable, political claim the real passage ↗.

In every appearance we can find — aggregators, social media, essays — the sentence travels without a work, a section, or a year. Wikiquote keeps it in the Disputed list for exactly that reason Wikiquote ↗.

Where a date is offered at all it is usually 1888, taken from a heading in The Portable Nietzsche. The underlying note is from autumn 1885–86. We could not establish any first-appearance date for the popular sentence itself, and have not invented one.

misattribution.truthLine: Not sourced to Nietzsche. The genuine note behind it says ‘it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations’ — and says nothing about power versus truth disputed list ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The added clause is what makes it quotable. ‘There are no facts, only interpretations’ is an epistemological claim; ‘whichever interpretation prevails is a function of power’ is an accusation, and it can be aimed at anyone who currently holds the floor.

That is why it circulates in arguments about media, science and history far more than in philosophy. It is useful in a way the real note is not — which is usually a sign that someone has improved a quotation.
context.detailsSummary: The real note versus the popular sentence
detailsBody: Nietzsche (KSA 12, 7[60]): ‘…no, it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations.’
The note continues about drives and ‘a kind of lust to rule’ — the only thread linking it to power.
Popular sentence: ‘All things are subject to interpretation; whichever interpretation prevails at a given time is a function of power and not truth.’
Variant: ‘…a function of power and not the truth.’
